title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
description: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed
body: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options."When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites. Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue"."Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation. "Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

schema.headline: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports

title: Molly Meldrum: King Charles and Elton John pay tribute to Australian music legend
description: King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.Meldrum's famil
body: King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011."Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special, saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death."His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour."As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room.""He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

schema.headline: Molly Meldrum: King Charles and Elton John pay tribute to Australian music legend

title: Uebert Angel: Prominent Zimbabwean preacher arrested on sexual assault allegations
description: A well-known Zimbabwean preacher has been arrested on indecent assault and sodomy allegations, local police said.Uebert Angel, who leads an internatio
body: A well-known Zimbabwean preacher has been arrested on indecent assault and sodomy allegations, local police said.Uebert Angel, who leads an international charismatic church with branches around the world, was arrested during a church service in Harare on Sunday. Pictures and footage of the dramatic arrest have since been circulated online.In one video, a convoy of vehicles is seen escorting the self-styled prophet as he sits in the back of a police van surrounded by armed police officers.The controversial founder of Spirit Embassy was also appointed Zimbabwe's special presidential envoy and ambassador-at-large to Europe and the Americas back in 2021 by President Emmerson Mnangagwa. In 2023, he made headlines when an undercover report by Al Jazeera claimed that he had offered to use his diplomatic status to launder large amounts of money through a gold-smuggling scheme in the country.According to the Qatar-based network, Angel, 48, told reporters working undercover that the scheme was approved by President Emmerson Mnangagwa.Zimbabwean police only released a brief statement confirming his arrest but a member of his team told reporters the British Zimbabwean national was still in police custody and it was unclear when he'd make an appearance in court."It can be in the afternoon or tomorrow [Tuesday]. We are still within the legal framework [for him to appear in court]," Professor Lovemore Madhuku told state-owned broadcaster ZBC in a clip posted online.This is not the first time the prominent preacher has been accused of improper behaviour.A report by local online publication ZimLIVE in 2021 said that Angel had previously faced allegations of sexual impropriety from several women, at least five of whom are in England. The charismatic preacher has denied the allegations, the outlet added at the time.Angel's church has branches in Zimbabwe, South Africa and the UK and he known for his ties to other African preachers like Malawian televangelist Shepherd Bushiri.

schema.headline: Uebert Angel: Prominent Zimbabwean preacher arrested on sexual assault allegations

title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
description: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities
body: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom."We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said."The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari."Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

schema.headline: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say

title: UK sanctions top Myanmar military leaders after Rohingya genocide ruling
description: The senior military leaders facing sanctions are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo.Miliband added that Myanmar's P
body: The senior military leaders facing sanctions are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo.Miliband added that Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing, who was sanctioned by the UK in 2021, is "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" as he was head of the military at the time of the genocide in 2017.He said: "Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again."Miliband also called for an "immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement".The foreign secretary confirmed that new legislation would be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.Last week, he expelled Myanmar's defence attaché after the ICJ ruled the country had committed genocide during the brutal military campaign in 2017.He told MPs on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, and there would be a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention, external.In its ruling last week, the court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal. Myanmar denied the claims against it.Reports said that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.Myanmar's leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi, was deposed by the military in 2021.MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan army were still happening.

schema.headline: UK sanctions top Myanmar military leaders after Rohingya genocide ruling

title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
description: Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.
body: Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes.""Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation. "We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy"."These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade. Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.If you have been affected by the issues in this story help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book

title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
description: Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe
body: Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't. The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch. Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism. Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga. Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia. The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern". Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

schema.headline: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war

title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
description: Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the
body: Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?One AI worker employed in the city is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity."In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn."Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking."It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn."Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory."The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

schema.headline: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing

title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
description: Image source, Hamza Z. H. Qraiqea / Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of ex
body: Image source, Hamza Z. H. Qraiqea / Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)ByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalemGaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the charity Oxfam says, external.Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards". Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contaminationOxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials."There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been clearedWith all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.The Israeli embassy sharply criticised the report, arguing that it relied on satellite imagery "and unverified assumptions, and its methodology lacks the academic rigour needed to withstand serious scrutiny".It said the report drew conclusions about Gaza's soil and groundwater without considering the excavation of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels by Hamas, rendering it fundamentally flawed.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent campsAlready, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps."There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."Image caption, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the warFarmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe."Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

schema.headline: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says

title: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failureByClim
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failureByClimate EditorSome may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday. The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Co-leader of the negotiations Chris Bowen blamed the failure to reach an agreement on "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory"Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty."For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.The wider political backdrop was still more revealing. The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.A majority that may yet offer hopeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, said a deal that did not mention fossil fuels was "unconscionable"Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action. So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received."This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the COP processSo is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary. Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are becoming increasingly competitive, while the upheaval in global oil and gas supplies is giving countries another reason to generate their own electricity rather than depend on imported fossil fuels.The energy transition is moving forward, whatever happens in the UN negotiating rooms. The problem is that it is not moving nearly fast enough for the climate.Figure caption, What’s next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?A rare moment of agreementPerhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept.The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold.This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger.Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond.And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take.That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.

schema.headline: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world

title: South Africa femicide: Night-time curfews and street patrols after women murdered in Ekurhuleni
description: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African policeImage source, Family handoutImage caption, Okuhle's body was fou
body: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African policeImage source, Family handoutImage caption, Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering studentByNomsa MasekoThuthuka Zondi and Eleanor Smallwood BBC World ServiceReporting fromEkurhuleniTuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured."When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten."It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBCImage caption, Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's deathOkuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years.There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South AfricaThe BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against womenIn response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested."It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received. The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South AfricaAccording to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change."I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBCImage caption, Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers."With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBCImage caption, Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap herKgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her."Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBCImage caption, Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistlesIn September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" -  after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later.It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group."We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBCImage caption, Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killedFollowing her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
description: Image source, Chris McGrath/Getty ImagesByJustin RowlattClimate editor and Esme StallardSenior climate and science journalistReporting fromAntalya, Tu
body: Image source, Chris McGrath/Getty ImagesByJustin RowlattClimate editor and Esme StallardSenior climate and science journalistReporting fromAntalya, TurkeyThe COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper. The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".The world is preparing for life beyond 1.5CThis was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, externalThe ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine lifeExtreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the worldImage source, Anil Shakya/AFP/Getty ImagesImage caption, In a 2C world extreme heat is expected to be experienced in every inhabitated area on EarthThroughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action."This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial, external and are not well advanced.Countries divided over approach on fossil fuelsThis year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago."The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states". Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.COP31 had some good newsMuch of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms. And some of those were agreed at the talks. The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits – money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases – will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.Renewable energy growth remains unstoppableWhat governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook, external points to another powerful force: energy security.It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.Image source, Costfoto/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesImage caption, Renewable energy capacity is expected to grow 60% more over the next six-year period than the previousThe economics have been changing too.Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities – this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity."We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".That doesn't make COP irrelevant.Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple."A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".Image source, Chris McGrath/Getty ImagesImage caption, Many are questioning whether the COP process is fit for purposeThe COP process needs to changeCOP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national climate plans, known as NDCs.Then came further agreements: a fund for climate damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.The international architecture for tackling climate change has, in other words, largely been built.Now comes the harder business of making it work. That's why this year's conference in Antalya, Turkey, had been billed as an "implementation COP".COP collapses: What's the future for climate action?The COP summit in Turkey has failed because of a row about even mentioning the cause of climate change. Is there a way the world can move forward with coordinated climate action?The emphasis now is shifting towards delivering commitments already made. Camilla Born, who helped develop the UK's strategy for COP26 and now heads the campaign group Electrify Britain, told the BBC this is making COP more procedural - less about fundamental negotiations than ensuring the machinery actually works.This could mean doing away with a cover text – the central political agreement that countries sign up to with new pledges.It is not a requirement to have one, and for many years countries managed without. Australia chose to push one for this COP, and it is where they fell down.On many of the procedural issues Camilla Born spoke of, they did agree things. That may be important. It isn't necessarily exciting.And there is a fundamental limit to what this machinery can achieve. Under the Paris Agreement countries have no mechanism to force them to meet their emissions targets.So, when critics berate the COP process for failing to tackle the problem fast enough, it isn't really the system that is at fault, says Alden Meyer, a veteran climate negotiator now at the climate think tank E3G.The COP process, he suggests, is "like a mirror that we hold up to ourselves every year". If the reflection is disappointing, the problem is the governments, not the mirror.

schema.headline: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31

title: On the streets with the French Black Block ultra left protesters
description: 'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra leftFigure caption, Watch: The BBC's Katya Adler speaks to protesters
body: 'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra leftFigure caption, Watch: The BBC's Katya Adler speaks to protesters taking part in recent demonstrationsByKatya AdlerEurope EditorFrance is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic.That's quite a claim – and one that needs examining.The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBCImage caption, The BBC's Katya Adler talking to a protester French intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article, external it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around €207m (£175.5m).Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed.Towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand.Image source, ReutersImage caption, French police pepper spraying protesters during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Paris earlier this monthAs we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they said.Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police – they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype."How can you justify the violence?" I ask them."Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard.""We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight."These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families.They weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry.Image source, Lee Durant/BBCImage caption, Left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block, tend to dress in all black, wearing ski masks or balaclavasEarlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement.I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks.They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again – would only speak if they could remain anonymous."Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society."How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered?They shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say.Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBCImage caption, Some protesters don't support the Black Block's violence but say the state's violence is worseFrench intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country.Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal.Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous.He showed me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt."We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me."We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw."I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve?As he's under 18, his parents give us permission to speak to him. They share his politics, Starflix tells me, but not all rioters - masked and dressed in black as he is - do."The Black Block isn't a single organisation. It's a technique. Some of us use violence to get government reform. I want to bring about a revolution."Other people are opportunists who use anonymity to steal things. When we all wear the same clothes, it makes it harder for police to identify us."When I ask if he is scared he might get hurt or arrested, he admits he is but says what frightens him more is the thought that society might not change.Social media plays a huge role in the riots. Starflix tells me he and his friends use Signal and Telegram to arrange to meet at protests.Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBCImage caption, "The Black Block isn't a single organisation," says protester StarflixThere are numerous websites and Instagram profiles, mainly hosted by left-wing organisations, offering tips for protesters and rioters, such as: keep your phone at home so police can't track you, cover your face to avoid being identified and emulate martial arts expert Bruce Lee and "be like water" - appearing and disappearing into crowds. That's advice passed on by the Hong Kong protesters eight years ago.While not formally organising the protests or violence with these posts, could the fact groups host this information online be viewed as a kind of incitement or manipulation of youngsters whose feelings are running so high in France?All the young rioters I spoke to insist they are not being herded or directed, but is there something bigger behind what's happening?Image source, Lee Durant/BBCImage caption, Ultra-left protesters spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymityIt takes our team a long time, but they manage to find a seasoned activist with the Black Block who would speak to us. I put to him Macron's assertion that the ultra left has organised groups that aim to bring down the French Republic. Is that true?"It's totally false of the authorities to say we are all organised. And the intelligence services know it," the activist scoffs. "It's a manipulation of the French public to make them think there is an enemy within.""Basically, people turn up to a protest, get dressed in black and do their own thing. The uniting factor is rage and not just in France. You see the same rage [in protests] in Italy, Germany, Spain. It's exploding by itself."I ask if the anti-capitalist presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party (LFI) are somehow linked to the violence. They are present at most protests, supporters handing out campaign pamphlets to the chanting crowds.But the activist denies this, telling me Mélenchon is "a capitalist because he's part of the system". He says the LFI and the trade unions try to "calm" unrest, while he believes things need to be "stepped up a notch".Why had he decided to talk to us, I ask - does he want to collapse the French government?"I just want to say we don't love violence. I don't want to destroy France. We want to destroy a system that is a capitalist system, of course, but to change the society in a way that we think will be better for the most people, for more people. "More and more find it hard to make ends meet. In the countryside, people can't even afford to fill their tank with petrol."You have to leave the city, heading out into the gloriously autumnal French countryside, to meet some of the more organised, hardcore elements of the ultra left.Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBCImage caption, Limoges Town Hall, allegedly damaged by protesters, has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be inThis is a world of eco activism and known saboteurs. One man remains in police custody linked to the fire during protests at Limoges Town Hall last month. The devastated, yet somehow still elegant, 19th century building has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in. An acrid smell still hangs in the air one month on.The 34-year-old arson suspect, who insists he's innocent, comes from a hamlet near Limoges, known for its anarchist, environmentalist community. His father, a fellow activist, is also known to French intelligence. We approached the father and the suspect's lawyer for comment. They didn't want to speak.Instead, we met a 39-year-old father of one, a local full-time ultra-left activist for more than two decades. Like the other individuals we spoke to for this investigation, he would only talk to us on condition he could remain anonymous."We were all shocked by the [town hall] fire – even as we watched it happen in front of us - but it's our duty to take action," he tells me."I can't leave this world to my son in the state that it's in. Look how military vehicles and brute force are used by the state against our young students."It's amazing the people haven't taken up arms against them. Do we need a policeman killed in order for the state to listen?"How can you say that, I want to know?"As a child, I was educated with French values – liberty, equality, fraternity - but when I look at the social injustice in the world now, I'm disgusted. As a father, I can't let this go on. If I have to, I would take a bullet to protect the youth of this country."These are dangerous-sounding words - but the radical left doesn't appear to be big, armed or united enough to seriously threaten France.Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBCImage caption, Upcoming presidential elections offer a crossroad, with polls predicting a run-off between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc MélenchonWe repeatedly approached French intelligence. They didn't want to comment. A sign perhaps of the huge sensitivity of the current situation, especially with France hurtling towards an extremely charged presidential election.But Michel Klein, a recently retired former police commissioner, told me he didn't think the radical left posed a serious threat to the French state."I believe there is a will from the radical left and the anarchists to try and destroy the Republic but they obviously don't have the means to do it," he told me.He sees no risk of civil war in France (a possibility you hear some in the country discuss these days) but he identified a rising risk of clashes between far-left and far-right groups ahead of the presidential election.Polls currently predict a run-off in the vote between nationalist candidate Marine Le Pen and anticapitalist Mélenchon.Far-right vigilante groups have begun appearing on the edge of protests in a number of cities across France to "protect French streets", they say.The popular hard-left presidential candidate Mélenchon attends most demos, his supporters handing political pamphlets to the chanting crowds, but he denies any links with violence.France is so polarised, there's little sign next year's presidential vote will calm things. This turbulent mix of left and right, social and political unrest, feels like a perfect storm.
